newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Bradys' days seen numbered as market evolves.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Bradys' days seen numbered as market evolves.

text.p: With the Philippines and Mexico sponging away the stigma of default by retiring their outstanding Brady bonds, analysts are starting to predict the demise of the $1,600 billion market.

Mexico amazed the international debt market in May when it issued a $1.75 billion global bond with a 30-year maturity and swapped the proceeds for collateralised Brady bonds worth about $1.24 billion.
The Philippines and Peru are following its lead, while Brazil, Argentina and Venezuela are all jostling to take the same path.
"I think we're going to see this as a growing trend," said Ousmene Mandeng, fixed income strategist at West Merchant Bank in London.
MARKETS MAY BE SET TO BLEND

"The Brady market is going to merge into the larger class of bonds outstanding. It's a natural process that started with the huge amount of Eurobond issuance since 1993, mainly from Latin America," he added.
"I very much believe it will become one market, probably within one year, as spreads contract."
Mandeng is not alone in predicting the end of the Brady market, at least in its current form.

Nicholas Brady, the former U.S. Treasury Secretary who masterminded the debt reduction plan that fathered the Brady market at the end of the 1980s, said last month he could foresee the demise of the market which bears his name.
"I hope all the Bradys go through the process, where the country stands on its own two feet," he told London financiers in the light of the Mexican move. "It's a sign of progress."

Last month the Philippines followed Mexico's precedent, issuing nearly $700 million in 20-year Eurobonds in exchange for outstanding Brady debt -- foreign commercial loans restructured into bonds after the 1980s debt crisis.
Analysts are still awed by Mexico's feat in launching such a long-dated issue of pure Mexican risk less than 18 months after its peso devaluation sparked a financial crisis.
Inspired by its success, Peru said two weeks ago that it too would buy back some of its Brady debt, though some analysts say it took that step well before making the announcement.
Now Brazil has passed legislation enabling it to follow suit, and analysts are betting on whether Argentina or Venezuela will be next to take the plunge.
Such an evolution is likely to see Brady bonds, which total around $130 billion with a 1995 trading volume of $1.56 trillion, traded in the same market as Eurobonds, and at comparable spreads.

Yield spreads between Brady bonds, and fresh debt the Brady countries have issued on the Eurobond market, have already begun to converge as their economies strengthen and return-hungry investors feel confident gaining exposure to pure country risk.

Researchers at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell (DMG) noted last week that the staggering growth in foreign reserves of Latin America, now brushing $110 billion, was fast approaching the $122 billion total of the region's outstanding Brady debt.
LATAM WELL ARMED FOR CHANGE
"This comfortable liquidity position...means that these countries are well placed to buy back their high yielding external obligations," said Paul Luke, DMG's head of emerging market research.
With its extraordinary accumulation of international reserves -- at $60 million it has more than tripled 1989's $17.5 billion -- Brazil is certainly one of the best placed in the region to do so.
But Richard Gray, emerging market analyst at BankAmerica, said that while these sizeable reserves do facilitate the buyback process, it is their quality above all that matters.

Brazil's reserve coffers have been swollen with so-called "hot money" -- short-term cash lured by the magnet of high real interest rates. But Gray said Brazil would be unwise to commit such short-term money to buying back long-term instruments.

While Mexico's reserves have also surged, much of that basket belongs to the United States and the International Monetary Fund, which bailed out the country in early 1995 at the height of its financial crisis.
Mandeng said if Brazil, which has some $57 billion in outstanding Brady bonds, were to take the buy-back route it was more likely to retire some of its high-cost domestic debt.
Brazil this week said it planned to do just that. But it puzzled some analysts who warn such a move may end up stoking inflation.
So what is the advantage to Brady countries in retiring this form of debt?
CHANGE OFFERS SPINOFFS

Apart from shedding the stigma of past default, buying back these bonds or swapping them for non-Brady debt allows them to lengthen the tenor of their outstanding obligations, or replace them with cheaper debt raised in the Eurobond market.
It also frees up the U.S. dollar component that serves as collateral within particular Brady instruments.

Par and Discount Brady bonds for instance, issued by Argentina, Bulgaria, Brazil, Ecuador, Mexico, Panama, Poland and Venezuela, were structured to contain zero-coupon U.S. Treasuries as collateral to guarantee their principal.
Retiring such instruments means the "zeros" can be released, cashed in with the U.S. Federal Reserve, and used for instance to buy longer-term debt.
How attractive that is depends on the structure of the instruments themselves.
"It's a function of the proportion of collateral to the cash value," Mandeng said.
But he said buybacks like the one Mexico achieved represent only a small proportion of the Brady market overall.
Mexico for instance swapped just $1.7 billion, while some $22 billion remains in its outstanding Par bonds alone.
But the natural amortisation of such debt instruments will also play a part as they reach the end of their natural life.
Nor will forthcoming reschedulings, like that Russia and the Ivory Coast are negotiating with commercial creditors grouped in the London club, add new Bradys to the market.

The instruments born out of such talks will be Brady-style rather than proper Brady bonds, since they involve no debt relief. The Ivory Coast is seen as the last significant debtor to agree such a deal, with around $3 billion under negotiation. --London Newsroom +44 171 542 2734
